executive_summary: EUR/AUD closed at 1.61773 on 2026-10-02, one session after the valuation date. One euro buys 1.61773 Australian dollars, and a rising rate means a stronger euro. The pair is up 0.19% over one month but down 1.78% over three months, 2.05% over six and 9.55% over twelve, and it sits at the 4th percentile of its 52-week closing range (1.60916–1.80259). The main story is a high-carry cross caught in an energy shock. The RBA's 4.60% cash rate is 210bp above the ECB's 2.50% deposit rate, and a rolled short earns a futures-implied 205.2bp a year. The euro area is paying the winter gas bill and carrying the French sovereign premium, while Australia collects coal and LNG export receipts. The two-sided picture is less one-sided than the standalone dossiers suggest (EUR Bearish -0.2651, AUD Bullish +0.3040). Euro-area data are now beating Australia's, the dollar effect cancels out in the cross, and fast-money and real-money positioning offset each other. The settled verdict is tactically Bearish at conviction 2 (net score -0.1801). It rests on a pricing gap: the euro curve prices more ECB tightening than the ECB's own guidance supports, and the Australian curve prices less RBA tightening than the RBA's guidance supports. Strategically the verdict is Neutral at conviction 2 (net -0.0860), because rates and external balances offset. On the chart, the moving averages are stacked bearishly: spot is below the 50-day (1.62559), the 100-day (1.63131), the 200-day (1.6519) and a rising 200-week average (1.66776). But spot sits inside the six-touch 1.6106–1.6234 support zone after three tests of 1.6079–1.6082 in September, so the near-term downside runs straight into a floor. Our main caveat comes from reporting after the valuation date: money markets now expect the RBA to stay on hold until at least May 2027. That narrows the Australian side of the tactical pricing gap. Risk/reward from spot is poor (base case +117 pips against an adverse case of -227), so the better entry is to sell rallies into 1.6225–1.6255 with a stop above 1.6350 and let roughly 27 pips a month of carry do part of the work. Strategically the edge is the carry, not the spot level: our probability-weighted six-month spot of 1.6163 sits about 180 pips below the derived six-month forward of 1.63428.

market_context.valuation_assessment: The two dossiers carry valuation measures that point the same way and differ only in degree. REER-relative proxy: on the BIS broad real measure, the euro's REER of 103.34 against Australia's 116.11 makes the euro roughly 11% cheap to the AUD; rescaled to the current spot, the gap would close near 1.818, almost exactly where the pair traded a year ago at the 52-week high of 1.8162. World Bank 2025 PPP: using German PPP as the euro proxy, the AUD is 21.4% rich to the euro, which implies a fair value near 1.9704, about 21.8% above spot. Both are proxies rather than true fair values, and neither has forcing power inside six months. What they establish is that the current level already capitalises the rate advantage: the AUD has gained 9.97% in real terms over the year while iron ore fell 7.14%. Spot at the 4th percentile of its range is therefore cheap for the euro on valuation and expensive for the euro on carry, which is the offset Factor 5 strategic records.

market_context.recent_regime: The cross ran one of its sharpest one-way declines in the spring: EUR/AUD fell for a twelfth consecutive week, its most bearish run on record, into late May as the RBA's tightening outpaced the ECB's. Over the last 30 sessions the pair broke from 1.64175 on 20 August to 1.61725 on 28 August, a 245-pip drop in six sessions. It then based between 1.6079 and 1.6228 through September. It rallied 224 pips from the 22 September close (1.60916) to 1.63151 on 30 September, the session after the RBA's hike and alongside the soft August Australian CPI, and then gave back 138 pips over 1–2 October to 1.61773. The driver has been less about rates than the differential implies: a June review argued that risk appetite has had a far stronger relationship with EUR/AUD than energy prices or rate differentials, with risk-on favouring the Aussie and soured sentiment favouring the euro. That is consistent with Factor 3's two-sided reading.

The futures-implied funding premium a rolled position actually pays is 205.2bp, from the CME 6A/6E calendar spread observed 2026-09-30, and it bundles the rate differential with cross-currency basis. Carry-to-vol is 0.359 on the policy differential over the estimated 3-month implied vol of 5.847% (2.10/5.847), probably nearer 0.31 because the vol estimate runs low; on the 205.2bp funding premium it is 0.351 (signed -0.351 for a long), and 0.435 on 60-day realised vol of 4.83%. But with spot at the 4th percentile of its range most of the directional benefit is behind it, and carry is now the larger share of what a short can expect to earn. Forward points are derived linearly from the 205.2bp premium and are not quoted.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: For EUR/AUD the policy differential is -210bp: the ECB deposit rate is 2.50% after the 10 September hike and the RBA cash rate is 4.60% after the unanimous 29 September hike, both confirmed by the gated rate block. The front end shows nearly the same gap, with the 2-year Schatz at 3.20% against the Australian 2-year at 4.98% for about -178bp. At ten years the gap is about -180bp on the dossiers' live prints (Bund 3.58%, ACGB 5.38%). The payload's monthly 10-year series give -183.5bp as of 2026-08-01, and those are not quoted as live. The level matters less than what is priced. The Schatz prices about 70bp of further ECB tightening above the cash rate, while the Australian 2-year prices only about 38bp above the RBA's rate. So the curve already expects the differential to narrow in the euro's favour. Both dated tests inside the four-week window lean against that narrowing. A hike on 29 October is priced under 30%, and the ECB calls its stance measured and decides meeting by meeting, so a hold trims EUR front-end pricing. The RBA's 3 November decision is priced near 20% after the August monthly CPI undershot. But the Board kept an explicit tightening bias, and the September-quarter CPI on 28 October lands first, which gives the AUD leg the more asymmetric repricing. The factor reaches the pair through the front-end spread and through carry: a rolled short earns about 205bp a year. Confidence is held at 55 because the AUD side depends on one CPI print and the 20% pricing already reflects a softer August.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the direction of the differential becomes genuinely two-sided. On the euro side, the modal path is one more ECB hike at the 17 December projections meeting. That narrows the actual policy gap by 25bp, even though it delivers far less than the roughly 70bp in the Schatz. On the Australian side the gated file schedules two RBA decisions in the window, 3 November and 8 December. Bank views range from a 4.60% peak, which Westpac and CBA held before the decision, to 4.85% from ANZ. Westpac's chief economist now expects another rise unless the Middle East conflict is resolved. Against that, unemployment at a post-COVID high of 4.6% and negative NAB business conditions invite the market to start pricing an RBA pivot early in 2027. If the ECB hikes once and the RBA hikes zero or one more time, the realised differential ends the horizon between about -185bp and -210bp. Each leg would then fall short of its own curve by a similar margin, so neither has a clear relative-pricing edge. The carry is already in the forward: a funding premium of about 205bp means forwards sit above spot, so carry pays a short only if spot holds still. That is a return on holding the position, not a fundamental reason for spot to move. Net, the rate channel is a wash at this horizon.

factors.horizon_split: The stance moves from Bearish to Neutral because the two horizons see different parts of the rate story. In the next four weeks the ECB decision (29 October) and the Australian CPI (28 October) both test a curve that already prices the euro side more hawkishly. That asymmetry leans against the pair. Over six months the likely ECB hike on 17 December and a possible RBA pivot as the labour market loosens both narrow the realised differential. Each leg also falls short of its own curve, so the relative edge disappears. Confidence falls only from 55 to 52 because the carry level is common to both horizons. Pass-2 note (does not alter the scored stance): The tactical case leans on the AUD side of the pricing gap staying live. Reporting after the valuation date points two ways. On one side, money markets were reported to expect the RBA to remain on hold at least until May 2027, after Governor Bullock said three hikes could be enough to push inflation toward target. On the other, one read of the press conference was that policy was already restrictive and the RBA was prepared to let the four hikes already delivered work through the economy. If that reading of the guidance is right, the gap the factor scores is smaller than scored. If the market has simply priced out the RBA further, the gap is larger. We record this as the most important unresolved question for the tactical verdict.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The gap in data surprises currently favours the euro. Euro-area activity is beating expectations: the September flash composite PMI printed 53.1 against 51.7 expected, a 41-month high, and Q2 GDP grew 0.6% on the quarter. Australian activity is missing them: the September composite PMI fell to 50.8 from 52.7, with manufacturing at 49.3. Australian unemployment rose to a post-COVID high of 4.6% with full-time jobs falling, and NAB business conditions turned negative for the first time since 2020. On inflation, the levels give the AUD leg the stronger case for further policy action: the trimmed mean is 3.6% against euro-area core HICP of 2.4%. But Australia's August monthly CPI came in below expectations and cut November hike odds to about 20%. Meanwhile the euro-area national September prints point to a hot headline flash, which MUFG tracks at 3.8%. Australia still leads on year-on-year growth, 2.1% against 1.2%, but the two economies are converging quickly. Surprises move front-end pricing. The releases that could move the pair most inside the window are Australian (labour force on 15 October, Q3 CPI on 28 October), and the August undershoot plus the labour trend tilt their risk toward soft outcomes. Confidence is low because a hot Q3 trimmed mean would flip the factor in one print and euro-area core is still falling.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months both economies absorb the same energy shock from opposite sides, and the cycle is turning faster in Australia. Australia's evidence is concrete. Purchase costs rose 1.2% in the quarter against final prices of 0.5%, so firms are absorbing the shock in margins, and NAB sales margins sit at -20. Business conditions are negative, wage growth of 3.2% means real wages have fallen for three quarters, and unemployment is rising under a 4.60% cash rate. That is how a cost-push shock turns into a demand contraction. In the euro area the energy shock is a real-income tax too: core inflation is falling to 2.4% and negotiated wages slowed to 3.0%. But the ECB revised growth up to 0.9% for 2026 and 1.4% for 2027, citing resilience, and Germany's 2027 budget raises spending 5.9% with defence at EUR 109.7bn. So the euro area is earlier in its tightening with fiscal support, while Australia is later, with restrictive policy starting to bite. Australia's growth lead is narrowing, and narrowing growth differentials move the cross over months, not weeks. Risk to the view: the euro area's energy bill rises through winter while Australia's export receipts gain, which is handled under Factor 5 rather than double-counted here.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: EUR/AUD is a risk-off pair by construction. The Australian dollar has the highest risk beta in the G10, while the euro is neither a haven nor a high-beta currency, so the pair tends to rise when equities and credit sell off and to fall in calm, carry-friendly conditions. The current regime gives no clean read. Equity volatility is low, with the VIX at 16.07 at the 28th percentile of its year, and the S&P 500 is up 14% on the year. Credit is fraying at the edges: US high yield widened 42bp on the month to 302bp, the 83rd percentile of its year, and investment grade sits at the 86th percentile. The shock in markets is a rates shock, with the US 10-year at 5.24% after a 51bp monthly rise, not an equity break. Both legs weaken against the dollar in that configuration, which tends to cancel in the cross. Superannuation hedging also mechanically damps the AUD's risk beta when global equities hold their gains. A credit-led deterioration from here would lift the pair, while a soft US inflation path that calms yields would favour the AUD carry leg. Neither branch dominates inside four weeks, so the honest stance is Neutral.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the risk channel is governed by how the Iran war resolves, and for this cross the two branches cut across each other. A Hormuz settlement would be risk-positive, which favours the high-beta AUD and lowers the pair. But it would also relieve the euro area's terms of trade and real incomes more than any other G10 economy's, which favours the euro and lifts the pair. A renewed closure reverses both effects: risk-off lifts the pair, while the energy hit to the euro lowers it. The China channel, which normally gives the AUD its pro-cyclical tilt, is weak rather than supportive. Q2 Chinese GDP of 4.3% was the slowest since end-2022, and the September NBS manufacturing PMI of 50.1 is one month above the line rather than an impulse. A Chinese stimulus package at the December Central Economic Work Conference is the one risk-positive event with a clean pair-negative sign, but it is unscheduled in the gated file and uncertain in size. Credit at the wide end of its one-year range is an early pair-positive warning, offset by low equity volatility. The distribution is wide and centred near zero, so the honest stance is Neutral with a fat-tailed caveat rather than a forced direction.

Non-commercial traders were net short both currencies at the 22 September report: 52,334 EUR contracts and 46,814 AUD contracts. The Traders in Financial Futures breakdown is more informative and contradicts itself. Nearly 90% of surveyed Australian super funds expect to raise FX hedge ratios, which means mechanical AUD buying. Euro asset managers cut 35,215 contracts in a single week, the largest real-money reduction in the cached series. Against that, the fast-money pair-short is where squeeze risk sits if the 28 October CPI is soft. With the two report families disagreeing within each leg, positioning cannot carry a tactical direction.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the stock that matters is the euro asset-manager long, and it is shrinking. At 216,483 contracts, about USD 30.7bn notional, it is roughly four times the size of any other book in either leg. It fell 14.0% in one week, the largest real-money reduction in the cached series. A continued orderly unwind is euro selling, and against the AUD it competes with the AUD asset-manager short of 55,353 contracts, which is far smaller in notional. The structural AUD flow points the same way. Australian super funds hold about half of listed offshore equity hedged, nearly nine in ten intend to raise ratios, and none expect to cut FX exposure, so persistent global equity gains convert into AUD demand. The offsets keep confidence at 50. The two CFTC report families disagree on both legs. FXE, FXA and Target2 flow data could not be sourced. And the AUD asset-manager short would become AUD demand if it covered. On balance the larger, slower flow is euro supply and Australian hedging demand, which leans the pair lower over the horizon.

Higher TTF gas is negative for the euro. Higher Asian LNG is often positive for the AUD. And Newcastle thermal coal at USD 145.20 a tonne, up 36.7% on the year, is a direct Australian export gain. The direct bilateral relationship is stable rather than moving: on IMF DOTS 2024 data the euro area exported USD 36.2bn of goods to Australia and imported USD 10.7bn, a USD 25.5bn euro surplus. Brent's retracement from USD 114.89 to about USD 98 in late September is partial relief for the euro, which is why confidence is only 52 on a 0.06 weight.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: At strategic weight the external accounts and the terms of trade pull in opposite directions hard enough to cancel. On the level of the external accounts, the euro is clearly stronger. The euro area runs a current-account surplus of 1.92% of GDP, while Australia runs a deficit of 3.67%, a 5.6-point gap. Australia's goods-and-services balance is itself in deficit, at AUD 5.1bn in the June quarter, and net foreign debt is AUD 1,486bn. Valuation reinforces that. Australia's BIS real effective exchange rate is 116.11, the highest in the set and up 9.97% on the year, against the euro's 103.34, down 1.01. On the REER-relative proxy that makes the euro about 11% cheap to the AUD, and World Bank PPP puts the AUD about 21% rich to the euro. The trajectory into winter runs the other way. The euro area is the G10's largest net energy importer, facing thin storage and a TTF price 43% above the ECB's own assumption, and its monthly current-account flow fell from EUR 35.1bn to EUR 27.6bn. Australia is a net energy exporter collecting coal and LNG gains, even as iron ore and China soften. Valuation rarely forces adjustment inside six months, and the winter energy bill is a forecast, not yet a print. So the honest strategic reading is that a strong-level euro and a strong-trajectory AUD offset each other.

strategic.what_is_priced: The pair embeds neither a valuation correction toward the euro nor a winter energy squeeze against it. Both are real and roughly offsetting over six months. Valuation is a multi-year argument for the euro, not an actionable strategic signal on its own.

net_commodity_exposure.base_commodity_profile: Euro area: the G10's largest net energy importer. Oil up is negative for the EUR (single minus), TTF gas up is negative (single minus, the dominant one this winter), and it has no material commodity export offset. Energy imports are EUR 41.3bn a month and up 13.9% on the year.
net_commodity_exposure.quote_commodity_profile: Australia: an exporter of iron ore (about 35% of export revenue, the double-plus driver), thermal and metallurgical coal, LNG and copper, and a net energy exporter in value terms. Oil up is mildly positive (single plus), JKM LNG up is sometimes positive, iron ore up is strongly positive.
net_commodity_exposure.net_effect_calculation: Step 1, oil up: EUR gets minus, AUD gets plus (mild), so the net is pair down. Step 2, TTF gas up: EUR gets minus and the AUD is unaffected directly, so the net is pair down. Step 3, JKM LNG up: AUD sometimes gets plus and EUR is indirectly negative through competition for cargoes, so the net is pair down. Step 4, iron ore up: AUD gets double-plus and EUR is mildly negative as an importer, so the net is strongly pair down. Iron ore down reverses it to pair up. Current state: energy is elevated (TTF EUR 72.90, coal +36.7% y/y), which nets pair-negative, while iron ore is soft (-7.14% y/y), which is a partial pair-positive offset. The energy legs dominate for the winter quarter.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_up_10pct: Pair falls. The euro area pays a larger import bill and its terms of trade worsen, while Australia gains mildly through LNG-linked export receipts. The EUR leg takes the larger hit.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_down_10pct: Pair rises. The euro area gets terms-of-trade and real-income relief, and the RBA loses part of its 'permanently higher' fuel rationale, which weakens the AUD rate leg as well.
net_commodity_exposure.dominant_commodity_driver: European natural gas (TTF) on the euro side through the winter, set against iron ore on the Australian side. The ratio of TTF to iron ore is the single best commodity summary for this cross over the strategic horizon.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Guidance is diverging in a pair-negative direction, and the divergence is between what each bank says and what its curve prices. The ECB adopted a meeting-by-meeting approach, said it is not pre-committing to a path, and Lagarde described a measured response on a middle path. She told Parliament on 30 September that the Bank does not react to energy prices as such and that wages show no material response. Schnabel, the leading hawk, made further moves conditional and said policy can tolerate a more gradual return of inflation to target. Yet the Schatz still carries about 70bp of tightening, so the euro curve is more hawkish than the bank. The RBA is the mirror image. Its 29 September decision was unanimous, it judged further tightening of financial conditions warranted, and it kept the option of raising the cash rate further if needed. Bullock called the fuel price rise permanently higher and the exchange rate the most important transmission channel, which gives the RBA no reason to talk the currency down. The market prices only about 20% for November, so the Australian curve is less hawkish than the bank. Both banks have credibility: the ECB has delivered two hikes and the RBA four this year. In the gated calendar the ECB speaks first, on 29 October, and the RBA five days later, so a dovish-leaning ECB hold sets the tone before the RBA can confirm its bias.

tactical.what_is_priced: The euro curve prices an ECB that keeps going, while the ECB describes a pause-capable stance. The Australian curve prices an RBA near its peak, while the RBA describes a live tightening bias. Resolving either gap toward the bank's own guidance lowers the pair.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the euro-side guidance gap is the larger and more durable of the two. The ECB's stated reaction function is explicitly asymmetric in this shock. It responds only to evidence that energy prices have become embedded in inflation, and both of the indicators that would show that, core HICP and negotiated wages, are slowing. Against roughly 2.8 priced hikes, one more hike at the 17 December projections meeting implies about 45bp of under-delivery. December is also the ECB's first chance to formally mark its EUR 51.0/MWh gas assumption to a market near EUR 72.90. The RBA's guidance is more coherent but less durable. A Board that has declared the fuel shock permanent has less room to look through inflation, which favours the AUD. But with unemployment at 4.6% and business conditions negative, the probability that it has to soften its own bias inside the horizon is meaningful. Westpac and CBA's pre-decision view was that 4.60% would be the peak. The 8 December RBA decision is the first test of whether the bias survives the October and November labour data. On balance the euro gap is roughly 45bp against perhaps 15-25bp on the Australian side, which leaves a mild pair-negative tilt at lower confidence.

strategic.what_is_priced: The curve prices both banks roughly as finishing their cycles, but the euro curve overstates the ECB's appetite by more than the Australian curve understates the RBA's. The net resolution is mildly pair-negative, contingent on the RBA's bias surviving the labour data.

The strategic case needs the RBA's tightening bias to survive a loosening labour market, while the ECB's shortfall against its curve plays out over December.

factors.weight_adjustment_reason: Tactical adjusted from the 0.05 default (+0.01). Event risk in this cross is unusually lopsided. The euro leg carries a dated domestic political binary (the French 2027 budget, with a six-week confidence fight running into the 17 November vote), while the Australian leg carries no domestic political event before May 2028. The +0.01 offsets the -0.04 on Factor 10 and the +0.03 on Factor 1 so the weights sum to 1.00. Strategic weight is the default.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Event risk in the next four weeks falls almost entirely on the euro leg. The French 2027 budget, with EUR 54bn of savings, was presented to the Council of Ministers on 1 October and faces a parliamentary vote on 17 November. France has had three governments in fourteen months, and the 2026 budget slipped from a 4.7% to a 5.0% deficit target before passage. The vote falls just outside the tactical window, but any confidence motion would fall inside it. Australia has no domestic political event: no federal election is due until May 2028, and no new Australia-China trade restrictions were identified. The Iran war is the shared event, and its effects are not symmetric for this cross. Trump rejected Tehran's seven-day reopening proposal and talks are reportedly stuck on sequencing. While that stalemate holds, the energy premium stays with the euro area, which pays it, rather than Australia, which partly collects it. Events also cluster: Australian CPI (28 October) and the ECB (29 October) land on consecutive days, which raises volatility, but a soft Australian print and a hawkish ECB are not the modal combination. The asymmetry argues for a mild pair-negative stance.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the event distribution widens on both sides and roughly centres. Three branches lower the pair. A French government collapse around the 17 November vote, with the 2027 presidential race led from both political extremes, would add a euro risk premium. A Chinese stimulus package at the December Central Economic Work Conference would lift iron ore and the AUD. And a renewed Hormuz closure would hit the euro area's energy bill hardest. Against these, a genuine Hormuz settlement would lift the pair materially. It would remove the euro area's terms-of-trade tax, which the EUR dossier values at +3 to +4% against the dollar, and it would also undercut the RBA's 'permanently higher' fuel rationale, removing support from the AUD rate leg. The settlement branch is therefore the one event that would push both legs in the pair-positive direction at the same time, which is why the distribution does not tilt clearly lower despite more bearish branches by count. Taking the dossiers' subjective probabilities (settlement 20-25%, French collapse about 25%, renewed closure about 15%, major China stimulus about 20%) gives a wide distribution with no reliable directional mean.

France's OAT-Bund spread is at its widest since 2012, against a triple-A Australian sovereign with 18.8% net debt, in a regime where global long ends are discriminating on fiscal quality. Offsets part of the -0.04 on Factor 10. Tactical weight is the default.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The fiscal differential is stark and currently in play on the euro side. The OAT-Bund 10-year spread closed at 111.2bp on 29 September, the widest since 2012. Its one-year range is 59.0 to 111.2bp and its one-year average 74.2bp. French debt is 119.3% of GDP and projected at 121.7% in 2027, the 2025 deficit was 5.1% of GDP, and Fitch rates France A+. The ECB's Transmission Protection Instrument is designed for disorderly dynamics, not for widening driven by fundamentals, so it gives the euro area's second-largest sovereign no mechanical backstop. Australia holds triple-A ratings from all three agencies with stable outlooks, net debt of 18.8% of GDP and a deficit of 1.6% of GDP, and has no rating review or fiscal event inside the window. The money reaches the cross through euro-area risk premium. Each leg of OAT-Bund widening adds to the euro's risk premium, with nothing comparable on the AUD side. The tactical weight is small, the confidence is held to 52 because the binary vote sits just after the window, and the published 111.2bp spread uses a Bund print 5bp different from other sources.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the sovereign differential is a structural euro negative against the AUD, with one genuine offset. France's debt path, its political fragmentation, a 17 November vote on EUR 54bn of consolidation, and a 2027 presidential field led from both extremes keep a risk premium on euro assets that the ECB cannot neutralise mechanically. Australia has more fiscal room than any economy in the benchmarking set. Net debt is projected at 19.9-21.8% of GDP through 2028, below its 2020 peak, and that room lets it cushion a slowdown driven by its own central bank. That matters because the global long end is pricing fiscal quality: the US 10-year is at the top of its range and the UK 10-year is the highest in the set. The offset is Germany. The 2027 budget's EUR 118.7bn of net borrowing, with defence and infrastructure funds outside the debt brake, will over time supply the deep euro safe asset the currency lacks, which is structurally euro-positive. But inside six months it mainly adds to Bund supply. Commodity revenue softening with iron ore is a minor Australian negative. Sovereign CDS could not be sourced for either leg.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: For a non-USD cross the dollar matters through each leg's dollar beta and through relative funding costs, and neither currently produces a clean signal. The dollar is firm on real yields rather than scarce liquidity. The Fed hiked to 3.75-4.00% on 16 September, the 10-year TIPS yield is 2.90%, and the broad dollar index is up 1.88 points on the month. Dollar plumbing is calm: SOFR fixed at 3.90% inside the target range, the balance sheet is expanding, and reserves are ample. Both legs sit on the weak side of a high-real-yield dollar. The euro is 57.6% of DXY and absorbs broad dollar moves mechanically. The AUD has the higher beta to the dollar and its banks fund offshore. Both effects run in the same direction against the dollar, so they largely cancel in the cross. The relative funding cost is visible in the payload: the futures-implied EUR/AUD premium of 205.2bp against a 210bp policy differential leaves a residual of about -5bp. assumptions: Price payload metadata, quoted as delivered: dataPoints 130; dateRange '2026-04-06 to 2026-10-02'; spot 1.61773; spotDate 2026-10-02; computationRange '2007-12-24 to 2026-10-02 (4900 weekday bars)'; dataQuality: 'EUR/AUD: 4900 weekday bars in the store (2007-12-24 to 2026-10-02); 1007 weekly, 483 monthly; 130 daily bars passed downstream (2026-04-06 to 2026-10-02), which is the 1-6 month strategic horizon'.

Spot date: spotDate (2026-10-02) is one session after the valuation date (2026-10-01). Every level, pip distance, percentage and forward is anchored to 1.61773. A later web-published ECB reference rate (1.6097 on 5 October 2026) is disclosed and not used; it would place the pair just below the 1.6106 floor of the six-touch support zone, so readers should check live spot against the 1.6079 triple-test level before acting.

Moving averages are simple averages of trading-day closes over the whole stored history: 50-day 1.62559, 100-day 1.63131, 200-day 1.6519, 200-week 1.66776. The 200-week slope is +0.000526 a week and spot has been below it for 25 weeks. Realised vol is annualised on 252 days (20-day 4.76%, 60-day 4.83%). ATR(14) is 0.00814, or 81 pips. The 52-week percentile is 5 on an intraday basis and 4 on a closing basis; the narrative and the range fields use the closing figures.

Zones come from the payload's clustering of weekly and monthly swing closes. The distances quoted are the payload's own and measure to each zone's midpoint; nearest-edge distances were computed separately against spot. Only three support zones exist below spot, so the support list is exactly the minimum (the support_levels field also lists the 1.6079 triple-test floor).

Chart pattern: the descending-triangle description is the author's own reading of swing highs and lows in the 130 bars. The opposing double- or triple-bottom reading is anonymous community commentary and is cited as such, not as bank technical research.

Rates and carry: the 10-year yields in the payload are monthly (EUR 3.18%, AUD 5.015%, as of 2026-08-01) and are not quoted as live levels. Carry figures use the gated policy rates (2.50% and 4.60%) and the 205.2bp CME calendar-spread premium. Forward points and outrights are derived linearly from that premium and are not quoted. The premium bundles the rate differential with basis, and the two cannot be separated without OIS curves. In the structured output annualised_carry_bps is signed from the long-EUR/AUD side (-205.2, a long pays) and carry_to_vol_ratio is -0.351 accordingly; the source's 0.359 and 0.351 are magnitudes from the short side.

Implied volatility: the cross's implied vol is the gated triangle estimate (atmIv3mPct 5.847% at 99.7 days). It runs low by 8.7–17.8% and is treated as a floor. The cross's own risk reversals and implied-vol percentile are unavailable (iv_percentile is null); CFTC percentile ranks for EUR and AUD were not provided in the source (base_cftc_percentile and quote_cftc_percentile are null), only thresholds relative to extremes.

Weights and the verdict: weight adjustments, all factor stances, confidences, evidence types and synthesis rationales are carried unchanged from the pass-1 verdict. Where the report disagrees, for example on Factor 9's chart reading and on the post-valuation RBA pricing, the disagreement is stated in clearly labelled pass-2 notes, and the scored verdict stands.
Scenario probabilities follow the 50/25/25 convention and are subjective. Expected values are probability-weighted pip outcomes from 1.61773, plus carry where stated.

Consensus sources: the NAB and Westpac AUD/EUR paths are relayed by a consumer FX publisher, are about four months old, and were not read from bank research. They are disclosed, not adopted. Aggregator forecasts (exchangerates.org.uk, Traders Union, CoinCodex and similar) are statistical extrapolations and are not treated as bank consensus, so bank_consensus_forecast is null.

Bilateral trade: IMF DOTS 2024 goods trade is used as supplied (euro-area exports to Australia USD 36.2bn, imports USD 10.7bn, net USD 25.5bn). The mirror figures differ, as is normal (USD 37.8bn on the Australian import side).

Dossier dates (base_dossier_date, quote_dossier_date) were not stated in the source report and are set to the valuation date; the China Central Economic Work Conference catalyst date (2026-12-10) is an approximation of 'second week of December'.
